arcChoices.title: Heroes and Epic Traditions
arcChoices.description: Eight weeks on heroic ideals, quests, war, tragedy, and changing versions.

arcChoices.title: Gods, Power, and Worship
arcChoices.description: Eight weeks on Olympians, divine families, cult, sacrifice, and contested stories.

arcChoices.title: Death, Underworld, and Afterlife
arcChoices.description: Eight weeks on Hades, katabasis, mourning, judgment, and heroic descents.

topic.iliad-anger-honor.title: Anger, honor, and consequence
topic.iliad-anger-honor.body: The Iliad does not begin with the whole Trojan War. It begins with Achilles’ anger and the suffering it causes. Read that opening as a study in honor: a heroic quality can be excellent and destructive at once.

cards.title: The war inside the war
cards.body: The Iliad opens with a quarrel inside the Greek camp, not with the fall of Troy. Achilles’ injured honor becomes a pressure point for the entire army.

cards.title: Excellence has a social cost
cards.body: Achilles is outstanding as a warrior, but his withdrawal harms the people who depend on him. The poem asks whether heroic prestige can justify communal suffering.

topic.odyssey-cunning-identity.title: Cunning, names, and disguise
topic.odyssey-cunning-identity.body: The Odyssey introduces its hero through ingenuity, travel, suffering, and return. Odysseus is heroic not because he is always stronger, but because he survives through intelligence, self-control, and carefully managed identity.

cards.title: The wandering mind
cards.body: The Odyssey’s hero survives by reading situations, changing shape in speech, and waiting for the right moment.

cards.title: Identity under pressure
cards.body: Odysseus’ false names and disguises show that identity in the Odyssey is something managed, tested, and slowly recovered.

topic.heroic-variants.title: When heroic stories change
topic.heroic-variants.body: Later mythographers reorganize heroic stories into readable systems. Pseudo-Apollodorus and Plutarch are invaluable, but they are later interpreters—not a single ancient canon. Always ask which source preserves which version.

cards.title: There is no single hero file
cards.body: Heroic stories move through epic, tragedy, mythography, biography, and local tradition. Each source selects and organizes differently.

cards.title: Later does not mean useless
cards.body: Pseudo-Apollodorus and Plutarch are later, but they preserve and organize traditions. The key is to label them rather than pretend they are ancient epic.

topic.heroic-tragedy.title: Heroes on the tragic stage
topic.heroic-tragedy.body: Athenian tragedy reshapes heroic traditions into immediate conflict. A play is not a neutral summary of myth: it chooses a version, sharpens the argument, and makes an audience confront the cost.

cards.title: Myth becomes immediate
cards.body: Tragedy turns inherited stories into a present-tense confrontation: arguments, choices, reversals, and consequences.

cards.title: A chosen version
cards.body: A tragedy does not merely repeat myth. It selects a version and sharpens it for a particular conflict and audience.

topic.epic-openings.title: Why epic openings matter
topic.epic-openings.body: An epic opening announces the poem’s real subject. The Iliad chooses Achilles’ anger; the Odyssey chooses an ingenious wanderer’s return. Those openings already tell us that heroism is not one fixed quality.

cards.title: The opening names the lens
cards.body: An epic’s first lines announce what the poem wants us to watch: anger in the Iliad, ingenious wandering in the Odyssey.

cards.title: Compare openings, compare heroes
cards.body: Reading openings side by side reveals that heroism is not one trait. It is the quality a particular story chooses to test.

topic.tragedy-reworks-myth.title: Tragedy as myth-making
topic.tragedy-reworks-myth.body: Tragedy keeps old stories alive by changing their pressure points. Euripides, Sophocles, and Aeschylus do not merely repeat myth—they stage competing duties, speeches, and consequences for a contemporary audience.

cards.title: Old stories, new pressure
cards.body: Tragedy keeps inherited stories alive by forcing them into contemporary conflicts about duty, power, family, and justice.

cards.title: Not a neutral summary
cards.body: A play can change emphasis, motives, and outcomes. Treat it as an argument with tradition, not a transcript of myth.
